summary: The note surveys global efforts to restore depleted coral reefs, starting with the Global Coral Restoration Summit in Sydney on September 15, 2023. It covers restoration science and methods such as fragmentation, larval propagation, gene editing for heat tolerance, community programs, and tech like ReefBots and 3D-printed reefs. It ends with financing, including the Reef Credit system, and data-driven monitoring.
one_line: Overview of worldwide coral reef restoration: summit commitments, farming and larval methods, genetic resilience, community projects, technology, and new financing.
key_facts: Coral reefs harbor a quarter of all marine life while covering less than one percent of the ocean floor.
The Global Coral Restoration Summit was held in Sydney, Australia on September 15, 2023, and ended with a unified declaration to implement large-scale restoration projects.
Dr. Eliza Kim, a marine ecologist from South Korea, warned: "Coral reefs are the canaries in the coal mine for our oceans."
Coral bleaching occurs when stressed corals lose their symbiotic relationship with algae, which supply much of their energy via photosynthesis.

Coral Vita, cofounded by Sam Teicher and Gator Halpern, popularized the coral fragmentation technique in the Caribbean in the mid-2020s, using land-based farms that speed coral growth by 50 times the natural rate.
Dr. Mia Hooper pioneered larval propagation at the Great Barrier Reef, which involves collecting gametes of spawning corals and raising larvae in laboratories before releasing them onto reefs.
Dr. Leon Hartman of the California Institute of Marine Science published a study on November 4, 2024, identifying a gene responsible for thermal tolerance in a rare Pacific coral species.
Gene editing to impart heat tolerance onto vulnerable coral species is contentious because of ethical considerations about genetic manipulation.
Project Coral Heritage, started in Indonesia on September 3, 2025 by Rizal Malik and Aisyah Putri, trains local fishermen in coral gardening to turn damaging fishing practices into conservation.
Underwater drones called "ReefBots" map reef structures, monitor planted corals, and in recent advancements take part in the planting itself.
Dr. Cynthia Liang led development of 3D-printed reef structures that emulate natural coral geometries to help marine organisms settle.
The Reef Credit system, introduced in late 2026, lets private investors fund restoration in exchange for carbon offset credits.
Global databases and satellite imaging are used to track the success rates of restoration projects.
